## Part A — Official Course Question Bank

### A.1 Official Sample Exam (`S1–S20`)

*Source: `131230--Sample of Exam Questions.pdf` (verbatim course sample set).*

#### Sample Question S1
Which of the following best reflects the Big Five trait of agreeableness?

- A) A high level of competitiveness and assertiveness in team discussions
- B) A preference for cooperative, trusting, and prosocial interactions
- C) A tendency to work best in solitary, analytical tasks
- D) A propensity to challenge leadership and resist feedback
- E) A high need for control and emotional impulsivity

> [!tip]- Show Hint
> Think about the interpersonal warmth dimension of the Big Five (`OCEAN`), contrasting high-agreeableness cooperation with competitive or antagonistic behaviors. See [Lesson 3](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3460-Obsidian/EXC3460%20-%20Organizational%20Behavior%20and%20Leadership%233.%20Lesson%203%3A%20Perception%2C%20Personality%2C%20and%20Individual%20Differences).

> [!question]- Show Answer & Distractor Breakdown
> **Correct Answer: B** — *A preference for cooperative, trusting, and prosocial interactions.*
> - **Why B works:** Agreeableness captures cooperativeness, warmth, trust, and good-natured prosocial orientation toward others (`R&J Ch. 5`).
> - **Why distractors fail:**
>   - `A` reflects low agreeableness / high dominance or competitiveness rather than agreeableness.
>   - `C` describes introversion (lower Extraversion) plus analytical focus, not agreeableness.
>   - `D` describes low agreeableness (antagonism/disagreeableness) or low openness to feedback.
>   - `E` combines high need for dominance with low Emotional Stability (high Neuroticism / impulsivity).

#### Sample Question S2
Which organizational structure combines functional specialization with project-based teams?

- A) Network structure
- B) Boundaryless organization
- C) Matrix structure
- D) Modular organization
- E) Flat structure

> [!tip]- Show Hint
> Recall which structure intentionally breaks *unity of command* so employees report to both a functional department head and a product/project manager. See [Lesson 10](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3460-Obsidian/EXC3460%20-%20Organizational%20Behavior%20and%20Leadership%2310.%20Lesson%2010%3A%20Organizational%20Theory%2C%20Structure%2C%20and%20HR%20Systems).

> [!question]- Show Answer & Distractor Breakdown
> **Correct Answer: C** — *Matrix structure.*
> - **Why C works:** A **matrix structure** overlays product/project departmentalization onto functional departmentalization, creating dual lines of authority (violating unity of command) to coordinate specialists across projects.
> - **Why distractors fail:**
>   - `A` (*Network* / *Virtual*) outsources major business functions to external partners around a small core organization.
>   - `B` (*Boundaryless*) seeks to eliminate internal vertical/horizontal chains and external boundaries altogether.
>   - `D` (*Modular*) resembles virtual/outsourced component assembly rather than dual internal functional-plus-project reporting.
>   - `E` (*Flat*) refers simply to few hierarchical levels (wide span of control), not dual functional/project teams.

#### Sample Question S3
Under expectancy theory, employee motivation is highest when:

- A) Rewards are externally imposed regardless of performance
- B) Employees believe effort will improve performance and lead to valued outcomes
- C) Managers issue frequent directives
- D) Goals are assigned without employee involvement
- E) Performance evaluations are standardized across teams

> [!tip]- Show Hint
> Vroom's Expectancy Theory multiplies three beliefs: $\text{Motivation} = \text{Expectancy} \times \text{Instrumentality} \times \text{Valence}$. What must all three links be? See [Lesson 12](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3460-Obsidian/EXC3460%20-%20Organizational%20Behavior%20and%20Leadership%2312.%20Lesson%2012%3A%20Motivation%2C%20Job%20Design%2C%20and%20Organizational%20Justice).

> [!question]- Show Answer & Distractor Breakdown
> **Correct Answer: B** — *Employees believe effort will improve performance and lead to valued outcomes.*
> - **Why B works:** "Effort will improve performance" is **Expectancy** ($E \to P$), "lead to outcomes" is **Instrumentality** ($P \to O$), and "valued" is **Valence** ($V$). Motivation peaks when all three are strongly positive.
> - **Why distractors fail:**
>   - `A` destroys **Instrumentality** ($P \to O = 0$): if rewards arrive regardless of performance, effort does not pay off.
>   - `C` describes directive leadership style, not expectancy-instrumentality-valence links.
>   - `D` relates to Goal-Setting Theory / participation, not Vroom's three cognitive links.
>   - `E` reflects procedural standardization in appraisal, not the three expectancy multipliers.

#### Sample Question S4
A team member holds power because they possess specialized knowledge and skills that others rely on. This is an example of:

- A) Legitimate power
- B) Coercive power
- C) Expert power
- D) Referent power
- E) Reward power

> [!tip]- Show Hint
> French & Raven divide power into formal (`Coercive`, `Reward`, `Legitimate`) and personal (`Expert`, `Referent`). Notice the dependency is built on *knowledge and skills*. See [Lesson 14](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3460-Obsidian/EXC3460%20-%20Organizational%20Behavior%20and%20Leadership%2314.%20Lesson%2014%3A%20Conflict%2C%20Power%2C%20Politics%2C%20and%20Negotiation).

> [!question]- Show Answer & Distractor Breakdown
> **Correct Answer: C** — *Expert power.*
> - **Why C works:** **Expert power** is personal power derived from unique expertise, special skills, or knowledge that others depend on.
> - **Why distractors fail:**
>   - `A` (*Legitimate*) rests on formal hierarchical position/title.
>   - `B` (*Coercive*) rests on fear of negative outcomes or punishment.
>   - `D` (*Referent*) rests on admiration, charisma, and interpersonal identification.
>   - `E` (*Reward*) rests on control over valued positive distributions (pay, promotions, praise).

#### Sample Question S5
A leader avoids making decisions, offers little direction, and frequently delays responses to team issues. This reflects:

- A) Autocratic leadership
- B) Transformational leadership
- C) Laissez-faire leadership
- D) Transactional leadership
- E) Servant leadership

> [!tip]- Show Hint
> In Bass & Avolio's Full Range of Leadership Model, which style represents the *abdication of responsibility* and active non-involvement? See [Lesson 5](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3460-Obsidian/EXC3460%20-%20Organizational%20Behavior%20and%20Leadership%235.%20Lesson%205%3A%20Leadership%20Part%201%20%E2%80%94%20Theories%20and%20Styles).

> [!question]- Show Answer & Distractor Breakdown
> **Correct Answer: C** — *Laissez-faire leadership.*
> - **Why C works:** **Laissez-faire** is the absence of leadership: abdicating responsibilities, avoiding decisions, and providing minimal guidance.
> - **Why distractors fail:**
>   - `A` (*Autocratic*) makes unilateral decisions and gives strict direction.
>   - `B` (*Transformational*) actively inspires, stimulates intellectually, and coaches individually.
>   - `D` (*Transactional*) actively clarifies roles, rewards goal achievement (*contingent reward*), or monitors deviations (*management by exception*).
>   - `E` (*Servant*) actively prioritizes follower growth and service, not avoidance.

#### Sample Question S6
A manager consistently treats employees fairly, communicates respectfully, and explains the reasoning behind organizational decisions transparently. Which concept does this best illustrate?

- A) Procedural justice
- B) Interactional justice
- C) Retributive justice
- D) Corrective justice
- E) Equity theory

> [!tip]- Show Hint
> Separate structural process rules from *how* a manager treats and informs people face-to-face (`interpersonal` dignity + `informational` transparent explanations). See [Lesson 12](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3460-Obsidian/EXC3460%20-%20Organizational%20Behavior%20and%20Leadership%2312.%20Lesson%2012%3A%20Motivation%2C%20Job%20Design%2C%20and%20Organizational%20Justice).

> [!question]- Show Answer & Distractor Breakdown
> **Correct Answer: B** — *Interactional justice.*
> - **Why B works:** **Interactional justice** is the degree to which employees are treated with dignity and respect (**interpersonal justice**) and given truthful, transparent explanations for decisions (**informational justice**). Notice both cues appear in the stem ("communicates respectfully" + "explains the reasoning ... transparently").
> - **Why distractors fail:**
>   - `A` (*Procedural justice*) focuses on the fairness of the formal *process/rules* used to determine outcomes (e.g., voice, consistency, bias suppression), whereas respect + candid explanations specifically define *interactional* justice.
>   - `C` and `D` refer to legal/punishment doctrines outside the R&J three-part organizational justice framework.
>   - `E` (*Equity theory*) evaluates perceived outcome-to-input ratios relative to a referent other, not respectful explanation quality.

#### Sample Question S7
A software development team continues to invest time and money into a failing technical solution primarily because of the resources they have already committed. Which decision-making bias is most evident?

- A) Overconfidence bias
- B) Anchoring bias
- C) Escalation of commitment
- D) Bounded rationality
- E) Representativeness heuristic

> [!tip]- Show Hint
> When negative feedback arrives but decision-makers keep throwing good resources after bad because of sunk investments or reluctance to admit a prior choice failed, what is it called? See [Lesson 13](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3460-Obsidian/EXC3460%20-%20Organizational%20Behavior%20and%20Leadership%2313.%20Lesson%2013%3A%20Decision%20Making%2C%20Emotions%2C%20and%20Organizational%20Learning).

> [!question]- Show Answer & Distractor Breakdown
> **Correct Answer: C** — *Escalation of commitment.*
> - **Why C works:** **Escalation of commitment** is sticking with a failing course of action due to prior sunk investments and psychological reluctance to admit error.
> - **Why distractors fail:**
>   - `A` (*Overconfidence*) is overestimating one's accuracy or success odds initially, not specifically continuing because of sunk resources.
>   - `B` (*Anchoring*) is over-relying on an initial number/piece of information when adjusting estimates.
>   - `D` (*Bounded rationality*) describes satisficing under time/cognitive limits rather than sinking extra capital into a known failure.
>   - `E` (*Representativeness*) judges likelihood by similarity to a stereotype/prototype.

#### Sample Question S8
Which of the following best describes the primary function of organizational culture?

- A) Eliminating all workplace conflict
- B) Reducing employee autonomy
- C) Providing norms that guide member behavior
- D) Increasing dependence on formal rules
- E) Enforcing standardized job descriptions

> [!tip]- Show Hint
> Culture acts as an internal social control mechanism ("social glue") that coordinates behavior through shared norms even without explicit rulebooks. See [Lesson 2](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3460-Obsidian/EXC3460%20-%20Organizational%20Behavior%20and%20Leadership%232.%20Lesson%202%3A%20Organizational%20Culture).

> [!question]- Show Answer & Distractor Breakdown
> **Correct Answer: C** — *Providing norms that guide member behavior.*
> - **Why C works:** Organizational culture creates shared meaning, boundary-defining identity, and behavioral norms/sense-making that shape employee attitudes and actions.
> - **Why distractors fail:**
>   - `A` is false: conflict (especially task conflict) persists in healthy organizations.
>   - `B` is false: strong cultures actually enable higher autonomy because shared norms replace micromanagement.
>   - `D` and `E` confuse *culture* with *formalization* / *bureaucracy*—culture substitutes for explicit written rules rather than increasing dependence on them.

#### Sample Question S9
In group settings, individuals tend to shift their judgments toward more extreme positions after group discussion. This phenomenon is called:

- A) Group polarization
- B) Groupthink
- C) Social identification
- D) Deindividuation
- E) Social inhibition

> [!tip]- Show Hint
> Distinguish *suppressing dissent to keep false harmony* from *discussion amplifying the group's pre-existing leanings toward either more risk or more caution*. See [Lesson 4](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3460-Obsidian/EXC3460%20-%20Organizational%20Behavior%20and%20Leadership%234.%20Lesson%204%3A%20Groups%20and%20Teams).

> [!question]- Show Answer & Distractor Breakdown
> **Correct Answer: A** — *Group polarization.*
> - **Why A works:** **Group polarization** (formerly *groupshift*) occurs when discussion amplifies members' initial dominant inclination toward a more extreme conservative or risky position.
> - **Why distractors fail:**
>   - `B` (*Groupthink*) is striving for unanimity at the expense of critical appraisal of alternatives, not specifically shifting toward *more extreme* poles after discussion.
>   - `C` (*Social identification*) is defining oneself via group membership.
>   - `D` (*Deindividuation*) is loss of individual self-awareness in large anonymous crowds.
>   - `E` (*Social inhibition*) is worse performance on complex/unfamiliar tasks when others watch.

#### Sample Question S10
A manufacturing team operates using standardized procedures and predictable tasks. Under Perrow's model of technology, this reflects:

- A) Nonroutine technology
- B) Engineering technology
- C) Routine technology
- D) Craft technology
- E) Adaptive technology

> [!tip]- Show Hint
> Perrow's `2 × 2` technology model crosses *Task Variability* (few vs. many exceptions) with *Problem Analyzability* (well-defined analytical search vs. unanalyzable intuition). Which cell combines **low exceptions** + **high analyzability**? See [Lesson 10](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3460-Obsidian/EXC3460%20-%20Organizational%20Behavior%20and%20Leadership%2310.%20Lesson%2010%3A%20Organizational%20Theory%2C%20Structure%2C%20and%20HR%20Systems).

> [!question]- Show Answer & Distractor Breakdown
> **Correct Answer: C** — *Routine technology.*
> - **Why C works:** Under Perrow's framework (and `R&J Ch. 15` routineness of technology), **routine technology** combines low task variety/predictable steps with high analyzability/standardized procedures.
> - **Why distractors fail:**
>   - `A` (*Nonroutine*) = many exceptions + low analyzability (e.g., exploratory R&D).
>   - `B` (*Engineering*) = many exceptions + high analyzability via technical formulas/manuals (e.g., civil bridge design).
>   - `D` (*Craft*) = few exceptions + low analyzability requiring tacit intuition (e.g., bespoke woodworking/art).
>   - `E` (*Adaptive*) is not one of Perrow's four technology quadrants.

#### Sample Question S11
Which leadership theory emphasizes inspiring followers through a shared purpose, intellectual stimulation, and attention to individual needs?

- A) Transactional leadership
- B) Transformational leadership
- C) Autocratic leadership
- D) Path-goal theory
- E) Laissez-faire leadership

> [!tip]- Show Hint
> Check the Four I's (`Idealized influence`, `Inspirational motivation`, `Intellectual stimulation`, `Individualized consideration`). See [Lesson 5](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3460-Obsidian/EXC3460%20-%20Organizational%20Behavior%20and%20Leadership%235.%20Lesson%205%3A%20Leadership%20Part%201%20%E2%80%94%20Theories%20and%20Styles).

> [!question]- Show Answer & Distractor Breakdown
> **Correct Answer: B** — *Transformational leadership.*
> - **Why B works:** The stem directly paraphrases **Transformational leadership**'s pillars: shared purpose (*Inspirational motivation*), *Intellectual stimulation*, and attention to individual needs (*Individualized consideration*).
> - **Why distractors fail:**
>   - `A` (*Transactional*) exchanges contingent rewards for compliance and monitors deviations.
>   - `C` (*Autocratic*) centralizes decision-making without developmental coaching.
>   - `D` (*Path-goal*) adapts directive/supportive/participative/achievement-oriented behaviors to clear obstacles along employee paths, rather than centering the Four I's.
>   - `E` (*Laissez-faire*) abdicates leadership altogether.

#### Sample Question S12
*(Official numbering/lettering `a–d` preserved)*
Dr. Ahmed notices that nurse Elena frequently submits patient charts late. Without checking the scheduling logs or speaking with her, he assumes she is simply disorganized and lacks discipline. Later, he learns that Elena has been covering double shifts while caring for a sick family member. Which attribution bias best explains Dr. Ahmed's initial judgment?

- a) Self-serving bias
- b) Fundamental attribution error
- c) Confirmation bias
- d) Actor–observer bias

> [!tip]- Show Hint
> When judging *another person's* behavior, we routinely over-attribute it to internal personality traits ("disorganized") and ignore external situational causes ("double shifts + family illness"). See [Lesson 3](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3460-Obsidian/EXC3460%20-%20Organizational%20Behavior%20and%20Leadership%233.%20Lesson%203%3A%20Perception%2C%20Personality%2C%20and%20Individual%20Differences).

> [!question]- Show Answer & Distractor Breakdown
> **Correct Answer: b** — *Fundamental attribution error.*
> - **Why b works:** **Fundamental attribution error (FAE)** is underestimating external situational factors while overestimating internal dispositional traits when explaining *someone else's* behavior.
> - **Why distractors fail:**
>   - `a` (*Self-serving bias*) is crediting *our own* successes to internal ability and blaming *our own* failures on external luck.
>   - `c` (*Confirmation bias*) is seeking evidence that confirms an already-held belief while ignoring disconfirming facts.
>   - `d` (*Actor–observer bias*) emphasizes the *asymmetry* between how we explain our own actions (situation) versus another's (traits); here only Dr. Ahmed's observer judgment of Elena is examined, which is the classic textbook definition of FAE.

#### Sample Question S13
Laura is the team lead for a product development unit. Initially, she made decisions alone and instructed her team on what to do. Over time, she transitioned to participatory planning, encouraged open dialogue, and integrated team ideas into final deliverables. As a result, team morale and productivity increased. According to OB research on leadership styles, what is the best explanation for this improvement?

- a) Employees respond better to financial incentives
- b) The team felt more included and valued in decision-making
- c) Stricter deadlines increased productivity
- d) Independent work led to greater individual autonomy

> [!tip]- Show Hint
> Notice the shift in Laura's style: moving from autocratic instruction to *participatory planning* and *integrating team ideas*. See [Lesson 5](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3460-Obsidian/EXC3460%20-%20Organizational%20Behavior%20and%20Leadership%235.%20Lesson%205%3A%20Leadership%20Part%201%20%E2%80%94%20Theories%20and%20Styles).

> [!question]- Show Answer & Distractor Breakdown
> **Correct Answer: b** — *The team felt more included and valued in decision-making.*
> - **Why b works:** Participative leadership and procedural voice increase intrinsic buy-in, psychological ownership, and morale because members see their inputs valued in shared decisions.
> - **Why distractors fail:**
>   - `a` and `c` introduce financial rewards and strict deadlines, neither of which changed in the vignette.
>   - `d` attributes the gain to solitary/independent work rather than *participatory planning* and *open dialogue*.

#### Sample Question S14
Sofia works as a junior analyst at a consulting firm. She has a stable salary, a permanent contract, and good relationships with her colleagues. Recently, however, she feels unchallenged and wants to take on more creative projects where she can grow her skills and contribute meaningfully. Based on Maslow's hierarchy of needs, which need is Sofia currently trying to fulfill?

- a) Safety needs
- b) Esteem needs
- c) Physiological needs
- d) Belongingness needs
- e) Self-actualization needs

> [!tip]- Show Hint
> Check which needs Sofia *already has satisfied* ("stable salary, permanent contract" = physiological/safety; "good relationships" = social/belongingness), then identify the top rung focused on creative skill growth and potential. See [Lesson 12](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3460-Obsidian/EXC3460%20-%20Organizational%20Behavior%20and%20Leadership%2312.%20Lesson%2012%3A%20Motivation%2C%20Job%20Design%2C%20and%20Organizational%20Justice).

> [!question]- Show Answer & Distractor Breakdown
> **Correct Answer: e** — *Self-actualization needs.*
> - **Why e works:** Physiological & Safety needs (stable salary, permanent contract) and Social/Belongingness needs (good colleague relationships) are satisfied; Sofia's drive for creative challenge, skill growth, and realizing potential is **self-actualization**.
> - **Why distractors fail:**
>   - `a` (*Safety*), `c` (*Physiological*), and `d` (*Belongingness*) are explicitly satisfied already in the prompt.
>   - `b` (*Esteem*) focuses on status, recognition, prestige, and external achievement rankings rather than intrinsic personal skill growth and creative self-fulfillment.

#### Sample Question S15
An organization launches a cross-functional task force with 18 members to design a new onboarding program. During meetings, a few members contribute actively while several others put in minimal effort, assuming the rest of the group will cover for them. Which group dynamic is most likely occurring?

- a) Group polarization
- b) Social facilitation
- c) Social loafing
- d) Groupthink
- e) Collective intelligence

> [!tip]- Show Hint
> In large groups (here 18 members) where individual accountability blurs, people systematically expend less effort than when working alone. See [Lesson 4](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3460-Obsidian/EXC3460%20-%20Organizational%20Behavior%20and%20Leadership%234.%20Lesson%204%3A%20Groups%20and%20Teams).

> [!question]- Show Answer & Distractor Breakdown
> **Correct Answer: c** — *Social loafing.*
> - **Why c works:** **Social loafing** is the tendency for individuals to expend less effort when working collectively—especially in oversized teams—due to diffusion of responsibility ("assuming the rest of the group will cover for them").
> - **Why distractors fail:**
>   - `a` (*Group polarization*) is attitude extremism after discussion.
>   - `b` (*Social facilitation*) is *improved* performance on simple/well-learned tasks when watched.
>   - `d` (*Groupthink*) is premature consensus suppressing dissent.
>   - `e` (*Collective intelligence*) is a group's general ability across tasks, the opposite of free-riding.

#### Sample Question S16
*(Official 4-option stem `a–d` preserved)*
Which of the following best describes coercive power?

- a) Power gained from personal charm and likability
- b) Power derived from knowledge and expertise
- C) Power based on the ability to punish or withhold rewards *(official lowercase `c` in PDF)*
- d) Power rooted in formal organizational authority

> [!tip]- Show Hint
> Match French & Raven's five bases of power: `c` corresponds to fear/punishment. See [Lesson 14](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3460-Obsidian/EXC3460%20-%20Organizational%20Behavior%20and%20Leadership%2314.%20Lesson%2014%3A%20Conflict%2C%20Power%2C%20Politics%2C%20and%20Negotiation).

> [!question]- Show Answer & Distractor Breakdown
> **Correct Answer: c** — *Power based on the ability to punish or withhold rewards.*
> - **Why c works:** **Coercive power** depends on fear of negative consequences—punishing, reprimanding, demoting, or withholding valued rewards.
> - **Why distractors fail:**
>   - `a` describes **Referent power**.
>   - `b` describes **Expert power**.
>   - `d` describes **Legitimate power**.

#### Sample Question S17

#### Technology Question T1 (Technology and gains in productivity)
A bank gives its advisers an AI tool that writes loan reports. For two years, nothing improves, because the advisers keep writing the reports by hand as before. Then the bank changes the job: the AI writes the reports and the advisers only check them. Within a few months, each adviser handles twice as many loans.
Which explanation of the organization's choice best accounts for this?

- A) Redistribution: one firm's gain is another firm's loss, so no new value is created
- B) Lags: new technology takes many years to pay off, whatever the firm does
- C) Organizational change and structure: gains come when the firm changes how tasks are divided, grouped and coordinated
- D) Mismeasurement: the gains exist, but standard statistics fail to capture them
- E) Technological determinism: the technology alone decides the outcome

> [!tip]- Show Hint
> Recall Brynjolfsson, Rock & Syverson's J-curve / Solow Paradox explanations in Lesson 11: why did productivity double *only* after job roles changed from hand-writing to AI-drafting + adviser-checking? See [Lesson 11](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3460-Obsidian/EXC3460%20-%20Organizational%20Behavior%20and%20Leadership%2311.%20Lesson%2011%3A%20Technology%2C%20Algorithmic%20Management%2C%20and%20Work).

> [!question]- Show Answer & Distractor Breakdown
> **Correct Answer: C** — *Organizational change and structure: gains come when the firm changes how tasks are divided, grouped and coordinated.*
> - **Why C works:** Merely installing AI yields the Solow Productivity Paradox ("investment without reorganization"). Only **complementary organizational restructuring**—changing division of labor, workflows, and coordination—unlocks the productivity surge.
> - **Why distractors fail:**
>   - `A` (*Redistribution*) argues total output never rises across firms, whereas here adviser output per person literally doubled inside the bank after workflow redesign.
>   - `B` (*Lags*) claims waiting *passively* pays off "whatever the firm does", contradicting the fact that two years of waiting changed nothing until the *job design* changed.
>   - `D` (*Mismeasurement*) blames statistics, whereas gains were zero until workflow changed.
>   - `E` (*Technological determinism*) claims the software itself determines outcomes regardless of organizational choices—the exact thesis this vignette disproves.
